items.scene: A worker was told to carry a laptop carefully, then ran down the hall and knocked coffee onto it, ruining the keyboard.
items.question: Who is blameworthy for the damage?
options: The worker, because they caused the harm through careless action
No one, because any accident removes blame
The laptop owner, because they owned the device
It cannot be judged because there was no intent
items.why_this_case_matters: Direct harm plus warning and careless causation makes this a clear blame case.

items.scene: At dinner, someone makes an awkward joke that embarrasses a guest, but nothing is broken, lost, or injured.
items.question: Is this a blame-for-harm case?
options: Yes, because any awkward comment counts as harm
No, this is mainly a tact or offense issue, not harmful responsibility
Yes, because the guest felt uncomfortable
No, because the speaker has a good reputation
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a near-miss that looks social, not a real harm-and-responsibility judgment.

items.scene: Two roommates argue about whether one should pay more for utilities because they used the shower longer than usual.
items.question: What is the main issue here?
options: Who is blameworthy for injury or damage
Whether the costs should be shared fairly
Whether one roommate is generally reliable
items.why_this_case_matters: This is about fairness and reciprocity, not causal blame for harm.

items.scene: A child runs through a room, drops a vase, and it breaks. No one had told the child the vase was fragile or that the area was off-limits.
items.question: Should the child be blamed for the broken vase?
options: Yes, because all accidents are blameworthy
No, not unless there is evidence of recklessness or clear carelessness
No, because the vase belonged to someone else
items.why_this_case_matters: This checks the shortcut that outcome alone proves blame; the accident is not automatically culpable.
